                                                                                                                                                   1
                                         COMMENTS OF
                              TEXAS ELECTRIC COOPERATIVES, INC.

         Texas Electric Cooperatives, Inc. (TEC) respectfully submits these comments in response

to the proposal for publication (PFP) regarding large load interconnection standards (LLIS).1 TEC

is the statewide association of electric cooperatives operating in Texas, representing its members

except as their interests may be separately represented.2 The PFP directed comments to be filed by

April 17. These comments are timely filed.

                                                I.       Comments

1.       Applicability Clarification

         TEC recommends that proposed subsection § 25.194 (b)(3) be clarified.3 TEC understands

the Commission’s intent that expansions of an existing interconnection should trigger these large

load interconnection requirements when the expansion causes the total interconnected load to

exceed a new 75-MW interval. For example, a facility currently operating at 125 MW that expands

by 30 MW to 155 MW would exceed the 150-MW threshold (75 MW + 75 MW) and therefore

should be subject to these large load interconnection standards. Evaluating applicability in 75-MW

increments aligns with the structure and intent of the underlying legislation.

         As currently written, however, subsection (b)(3) could be interpreted in ways that do not

reflect that intent. The phrase “an expanded interconnection that exceeds 75 MW by 75 MW or

more” could be interpreted to mean that the expansion itself must be at least 75 MW to trigger

§ 25.194, allowing existing large loads to expand repeatedly in increments below 75 MW without



1
  Proposal for Publication of New 16 TAC §25.194 (Mar. 12, 2026) (PFP).
2
  TEC’s 76 members include distribution cooperatives that provide retail electric utility service to approximately
5,000,000 consumers in statutorily authorized service areas that encompass more than half of the total area of the state.
TEC’s G&T members generally acquire generation resources and power supply for their member distribution
cooperatives and deliver electricity to them at wholesale.
3
  PFP at 7 (Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(b)(3)).


                                                                                                                       2
 meeting these requirements. Alternatively, it could be interpreted to require compliance for any

expansion once an interconnection exceeds 150 MW, even for small additions that should not

necessitate a new interconnection agreement. Neither of these interpretations appears consistent

with the Legislature’s purpose of ensuring grid reliability.

       To ensure clarity and alignment with legislative intent, TEC recommends revising

subsection (b)(3) as follows:

               (3)    an expanded interconnection that results in the total load at a

                      single site reaching a new multiple of 75 MW.

       TEC would also appreciate clarity regarding the applicability of rule to large loads in the

interconnection queue. It is currently unclear if these standards will apply only to large loads that

entered the queue following the effective date of Senate Bill 6 or to those that enter the queue

following the effective date of these proposed rules.

2.     Treatment of Load that Exceeds Contracted Peak Demand

       Proposed § 25.194 (b)(3), without additional guardrails, also creates the incentive for loads

to increase demand without seeking to expand the contracted peak demand established in an

interconnection agreement. For example, a load that requests an interconnection of 100 MW but

over time peaks above that, even to 174 MW without requesting changes to the interconnection

agreement and being incorporated in the interconnection process for the additional load, may

create additional transmission improvement needs that were not securitized, or utilize capacity

ERCOT intended for other, secured parties. Notably in (g)(2), regardless of whether the large load

withdraws its project in total or wants to lower its contract demand by some minor amount, the

rule requires the transmission service provider (TSP) or distribution service provider (DSP) to




                                                                                                    3
 draw down on the financial security.4 There is no alternative, and there is no way to allow for the

security to be maintained with minimum billing standards that reflect the lesser demand and

compensates other customers to hold them harmless from the increased cost for the slightly

underutilized assets. Similarly, under (h)(2), if the large load is 1 kW under the contracted demand

6 months after its deadline to meet its contracted demand, or after a milestone in the load ramp,

the TSP or DSP must draw on the security.5 There is no opportunity for the large load to pay a

minimum amount that is compensatory for the other customers, rather than having a letter of credit

drawn upon—even though it is recognized that any large load’s projected peak demand and ramps

will not be exact.

        If, on the other hand, the large load has a higher peak than requested, it may exceed the

capabilities of the transmission and distribution improvements. Without any operational

requirements on the large load, as those have been removed from the rule, it is unclear how ERCOT

will resolve this added, unplanned load.        ERCOT should have curtailment rights or fixed

withdrawal limits for non-emergency periods for large load use of the grid that exceeds its

contracted peak demand included in an executed interconnection agreement. In subsection (e)(4)

language should be added that requires large load customer to request additional capacity in order

to exceed its load ramp schedule or contracted peak demand, and that any load in excess of its

contracted peak demand may be shed by the TSP, DSP or ERCOT or otherwise limited.

        In order to clarify the applicability of the rule and meet the intention of the Legislature,

TEC recommends using the following language at the end of proposed (e)(4)6 before the “.”:




4
  PFP at 27 (Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(g)(2)).
5
  PFP at 28 (Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(h)(2)).
6
  PFP at 18 (Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(e)(4)).


                                                                                                  4
                , and the large load must apply for an increase in its contracted peak

               demand and ramp rates through an amendment to its interconnection

               agreement, recognizing that any demand that exceeds its contracted

               peak demand or ramp schedule is subject to load shedding by

               ERCOT or the interconnecting TSP or DSP.

3.     Study Responsibilities

       TEC also recommends that clarification be provided on which entity is to perform

particular studies. For example, an interconnecting TSP and interconnecting DSP and ERCOT are

all charged with studies. Additionally, there are situations where the TSP which has performed

certain studies will not be the TSP which ultimately builds the direct interconnection with the large

load. This is a common scenario in areas where another TSP’s lines cross the service territory of

a distribution cooperative. In that situation, the other TSP would be likely be tasked with

performing some studies, but the transmission cooperative would ultimately provide the

interconnection with the large load unless it connects at distribution voltage. The rule needs to be

clear which entities will perform which studies or direct ERCOT to adopt procedures to identify

those responsibilities.

       It is not clear what role the TSP or DSP will play in conducting some of the studies

necessary for Batch Zero or later studies, but there should be a clear demarcation of responsibility

to avoid additional costs and duplicative work. The rule should clarify that some parts of the

studies are performed by the TSP or DSP.        TSPs and DSPs must perform studies in order to

accurately identify the requirements of long lead time items and to provide accurate

interconnection cost estimates. TEC interprets this cost as the cost of transmission expansion

resulting from, but not directly attributable to, a particular large load, and when combined with




                                                                                                   5
 other large loads in the Batch Study, will not be known until after the Batch Study is refined.

Further clarity on what these costs encompass and whether they are allocated on a load ratio share

to all loads in the Batch Study would assist electric providers with determining accurate financial

security for system costs. TEC notes that transmission cost allocation is currently being assessed

in Project 58484 and further recommends that provisions to accomplish a fair allocation of these

costs established in this rulemaking align with those being considered other Commission projects.

4.       Clarity on the Definition of Certain Costs and Alignment of Transmission Cost
         Allocation Between Projects

The PFP references several different categories of costs and payments, including study fees,

interconnection fees, contribution in aid of construction, security for long-lead time significant

equipment, and security for system upgrades. While study fees and costs for significant equipment

can be estimated by the utility, and interconnection fees are specified in the rule, the costs of system

upgrades that must be securitized by the large load pursuant to the interconnection agreement is

not defined and may be difficult to quantify. TEC interprets this cost as the cost of transmission

expansion resulting from, but not directly attributable to, the large load. Further clarity on what

these costs encompass would assist electric providers with determining accurate financial security

for system costs. Additionally, how should interconnection costs be allocated if a large load and a

generator which will operate independently of each other are both being built at the same

interconnection point? TEC notes that transmission cost allocation is currently being assessed in

Project 58484 and further recommends that provisions to accomplish a fair allocation of these costs

established in this rulemaking align with those being considered in the other projects.

5.      Necessity of Maintaining Involvement of the Distribution Service
        Provider (DSP)




                                                                                                      6
            The PFP correctly identifies the interconnecting DSP as the exclusive entity certificated to

provide retail electric delivery service at the location where the large load seeks to interconnect. 7

The PFP also appropriately allows DSPs and TSPs to cooperate in defining their respective roles

in the interconnection process.8 TEC supports maintaining DSP participation in both the

intermediate and interconnection agreements because DSPs are the sole entities authorized under

the Public Utility Regulatory Act to provide retail delivery service to loads located in their

certificated service areas. As a result, DSP involvement is not optional; any agreement governing

service to a retail customer necessarily implicates the DSP’s exclusive rights and obligations.

           Any proposal to remove the DSP from this process must be rejected because it would

undermine a foundational element of the ERCOT market design under which retail delivery service

is provided exclusively by the certificated DSP. Excluding the DSP would impair its ability to

fulfill its legal duties, jeopardize system planning and reliability at the distribution level, and

potentially deprive the DSP of its rights established under its certificate of convenience and

necessity. For these reasons, any proposal to diminish or bypass local DSP involvement must be

rejected.

           Additionally, in proposed (d) and (f), it should be made clear that the DSP retains ultimate

ownership and control over any distribution infrastructure installed and operated in the

interconnection process, unless otherwise agreed to with the TSP. The DSP still bears

responsibility for meeting load shed obligations, including any emergency curtailments impacting

the large load. As such, the ownership and control of the distribution infrastructure not owned by

the large load is essential for the DSP. TEC recommends inclusion of the following sentence in

both proposed subsection (d) and subsection (f):


7
    PFP at 8 (Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(c)(4)).
8
    PFP at 9 and 18 (Proposed 16 TAC §§ 25.194(d)) & 25.194(f)).


                                                                                                     7
                    The interconnecting DSP, if different from the interconnecting TSP,

                   may retain ownership and control over any distribution assets

                   necessary to interconnect the large load, excluding distribution

                   equipment and transformers owned by a large load.

6.         Financial Security and Refund Scenarios

           It is essential that ERCOT only plans for legitimate large loads that have a high likelihood

of sustained operations. It is also essential that new large load consumers bear the direct costs

associated with their interconnections to and use of the transmission system and that cost shifting

to other consumer classes be avoided. TEC is therefore generally supportive of the financial

security requirements placed on potential large load consumers throughout the proposed rule.

However, TEC is concerned that the posting of a large financial security requirement prior to the

completion of an interconnection study is overly punitive, because at this point the load lacks full

information on the potential costs associated with the interconnection and the transmission

capacity that ERCOT will allocate to the load.

           The potential for forfeiting large payments is substantial. Large loads that do not enter into

an interconnection agreement within 30 days of the completion of the study or that miss certain

milestones after entering an interconnection agreement would forfeit 80% of all security

payments.9 TEC notes that there may be legitimate factors beyond the load’s control that cause it

to miss a milestone or the 30-day interconnection deadline. From the electric provider perspective,

the 30-day deadline may also pose challenges for smaller entities and inhibit thorough due

diligence. TEC therefore recommends lowering and making refundable the financial security

requirement for the pre-study intermediate agreement to allow large load consumers and utilities



9
    See PFP at 15-16 (Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(d)(10)).


                                                                                                       8
 to progress through the appropriate studies before large and binding financial commitments are

required. After the study is complete, TEC also recommends that the Commission allow for a more

reasonable timeframe for entities to enter into an interconnection agreement by lengthening the

period to 60 calendar days, allowing all parties to complete necessary due diligence without the

pressure of a quick deadline.

           TEC believes that the ability to demonstrate financial surety is key to being able to

participate in the batch study process to avoid shifting more of the cost burden to other loads if the

large load does not execute an interconnection agreement. Upfront, refundable financial security

will serve to remove speculative or questionable loads from the load forecast, while also supporting

business development for serious developers.

           If, after ERCOT study, the load subsequently enters into an interconnection agreement, the

PFP requires payment of an interconnection fee. Should the Commission maintain an upfront

financial security that is equal to or less than the interconnection fee (currently both set at

$50,000/MW), TEC notes that there will be no refund or other use of the security if the customer

proceeds with an interconnection agreement, because the security payment is drawn down to pay

for the interconnection fee.10 If the interconnection fee is not more than the security payment, there

is no need for the large load to pay the interconnection fee at the execution of the interconnection

agreement, because it will be deducted from the load’s security payment. Additionally, given that

the refund amounts will, for the first time, include netting of ERCOT’s costs and there is no

procedure in place to determine those costs or to have the TSP or DSP notified of such costs, this

will likely increase the time to provide refunds to loads, which points to the need for a longer

timeline for entities to enter an interconnection agreement.



10
     PFP at 23 (Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194 (f)(7)(A)).


                                                                                                    9
            TEC further recommends that in addition to the requirements for letters of credit as a posted

form of security listed in the proposed rule in subsection (d)(11)(C)(iii), the rule should clarify that

the form of the letter of credit must be acceptable to the DSP or TSP, as applicable, so as to avoid

the risk that certain terms included result in the TSP or DSP being unable to draw down on the

security. This DSP and TSP acceptance should also include the approval of the bank and not just

the credit requirements for a bank.

           Finally, there are several places in the proposed rule which reference drawing on security.

The Transmission/Distribution Service Provider (TDSP) or the large load customer might prefer,

especially in the case of a letter of credit, to have the TDSP invoice the large load customer for the

amount owed and return the letter of credit once the invoice has been paid. The rule should be

clarified to allow this practice.

7.         Offsetting TSP Rate Base

           Throughout the proposed rule TSPs are instructed to use funds from the large load

consumer to offset their costs in rate base. 11 While TEC understands and supports the general

intention behind these provisions to prevent large load costs from being passed along to other

consumers, TEC is opposed to these provisions as mandated rate base offsets, because removing

these costs entirely from rate base will also prevent the utility from earning a return on facilities

and equipment on which it is statutorily authorized to earn such a return. A TSP’s ability to earn a

rate of return on its rate base is critical to its ability to function as a TSP.

           The current draft does not require large loads to pay for the on-going costs of operating

and maintaining transmission built to serve large loads or the costs of upgrades. TEC supports this

position. Administration of charges for O&M costs assessed to large loads would be burdensome.



11
     PFP at 23, 27, and 29 (Proposed 16 TAC §§ 25.194(f)(7)(B), 25.194(g)(4), & 25.194(h)(4)).


                                                                                                     10
 Furthermore, once the transmission equipment is built, it will likely benefit the entire grid. Utilities

should therefore be able to recover the associated costs of the upgrades to and operation and

maintenance of these facilities as part of their rates.

        Additionally, for some transmission providers, these large rate base offsets may

significantly eat into the overall rate base of the utility, reducing or in some cases potentially

eliminating its rate base entirely, significantly skewing the utility’s financial standing. Even a

larger TSP may be detrimentally impacted by this requirement given the number of large loads

which have indicated interest in interconnection. For example, if a TSP signs interconnection

agreements for just ten large loads of 1,000 MW each, that would be $500,000,000 in fees collected

(10 X 1,000 MW X $50,000/MW). This could easily be half of a TSP’s rate base.

        While the TSP would still be collecting the fees from the large loads, collection of the fees

is far different than earning a rate of return on rate base. A TSP would only be able to earn interest

on the money deposited, a percentage significantly lower than the typical TSP rate of return. A

TSP’s debt service requirements are based upon expected rate recovery. A significant reduction in

rate base may, therefore, lead to a violation of a TSP’s loan covenants, putting its financing, and

thus, its financial future, in jeopardy. Additionally, the TSP would have insufficient funds to

design, construct, maintain and operate its system. The TSP would not have the ability to raise its

rates to support its necessary activities without a rate proceeding in front of the Commission. If a

TSP must raise its rates to continue to operate, then the benefit of any offset would be defeated.

        Even if the fees collected were lowered and the risk of financial impact to TSPs averted,

the additional administration of any sort of offset would be a significant additional accounting

burden for every TSP in the ERCOT region which received the fees. The offset would require

special accounting treatment and would need to be recovered over the course of many years.




                                                                                                     11
         There are numerous options available to offset the costs to other consumers for the

interconnection of a large load that do not impact the TSP rate base. These options range from an

offsetting of the ERCOT administration fee that can then be ultimately credited back to consumers,

or an offset to the annual TCOS charges. TEC is not advocating for any specific credit or offset

policy but recommends that the Commission consider taking this specific issue into consideration

through a separate rulemaking to fully vet all of the available options and ensure that consumers

are protected while TSPs have the funding necessary to operate and maintain the transmission

system.

        Clarity is also needed for when a large load leaves the interconnection process, and ERCOT

is charged with re-allocating what has become underutilized capacity. The new load to which the

underutilized capacity is allocated must also post surety to avoid leaving a gap in posted security

for the upgrades. The current draft of the rule does not specifically cover this gap and makes it

much more likely that the additional amounts will be recovered through existing mechanisms—

other customers—rather than the large load that steps into the shoes of the large load that has exited

the process.

8.      Contribution In Aid of Construction (CIAC)

        TEC reiterates and maintains its prior positions that it is not appropriate to impose a

recovery method for the direct costs of the interconnection on electric cooperatives and

municipally owned utilities (MOU).12 Electric cooperatives and MOUs continue to retain sole

jurisdiction over their rates and methods of recovery.13 Senate Bill 6 added an additional provision

to protect cooperatives and MOUs in PURA § 35.004(c-2), which specifically reinforces electric



12
   Comments of Texas Electric Cooperatives, Inc. at 7-8 (Dec. 19, 2025); Post-Workshop Comments of Texas Electric
Cooperatives, Inc. at 3 (Jan. 16, 2026).
13
   See PURA § 41.055(1)


                                                                                                              12
 cooperatives’ and MOUs’ rights to determine how they pass along large load interconnection

costs.14 Generally, when specific statutory language conflicts or contradicts more general statutory

language, the specific language controls.15 So while, in general, transmission rates are under the

jurisdiction of the Commission,16 in this specific case of large load interconnections, cooperatives

and MOUs are given specific, dedicated rights to pass along the costs of the interconnection in a

manner of their own choosing.17 To find otherwise would render PURA § 35.004(c-2)

meaningless.

        For example, an electric cooperative or MOU may prefer to hold financial security until

such time as costs have been incurred and then bill the large load for the actual costs incurred as

CIAC. CIAC paid in advance of costs incurred, absent strong regulatory provisions to the contrary,

is likely to function much like a cash deposit in the event of a developer bankruptcy. Electric

cooperatives should, therefore, be permitted to manage their financial security risks as they see fit.

        There are also practical reasons supporting electric cooperatives and the need to maintain

autonomy over how these costs are passed along. Electric cooperatives are required under federal

law to receive at least 85% of their income from their membership, commonly known as the 85/15

rule.18 A large load consumer will take retail service from a distribution cooperative, meaning they

are the member of that distribution cooperative. The membership of a generation and transmission

cooperative consists of its component distribution cooperatives. If a transmission cooperative is

required to accept direct CIAC, or other required payments under this rule, directly from the large


14
   PURA § 35.004 (c-2) (“An electric cooperative or municipally owned utility that has not adopted customer choice
shall pass through to a large load customer who is subject to the standards adopted under Section 37.0561 the
reasonable costs to interconnect the large load in a manner determined by the electric cooperative or municipally
owned utility.”) (emphasis added).
15
   See Harris County v. S.K. & Bros., Inc., No. 14-17-00984-CV, 2019 WL 5704244, at *9 (Tex. App.—Houston
[14th Dist.] Nov. 5, 2019, pet. denied).
16
   See PURA §§ 35.001, 35.004, and 41.055(1).
17
   PURA § 35.004(c-2).
18
   Internal Revenue Code § 501(c)(12)(A).


                                                                                                               13
 load consumer who is not a member of the transmission cooperative, the transmission

cooperative’s tax-exempt status could be impacted. Electric cooperatives will likely have to work

out individual payment processes where the distribution cooperative either acts as an intermediary

as the member of the generation and transmission cooperative, or payment made from the large

load consumer is styled as “on behalf of” the distribution cooperative. These concerns justify the

Legislature’s careful choice of language in PURA § 35.004(c-2).

           In short, cooperatives and MOUs must pass along the costs of interconnection, but they

still maintain the exclusive right to determine how those costs are passed to the large loads. As

such, proposed subsection (f)(9) should not be mandatory for cooperatives and MOUs and should

clarify that costs for cooperatives and MOUs must be paid for by the large load in a manner

determined by the interconnecting cooperative or MOU.19 This would bring the proposed rule into

compliance with its underlying statutory authority and reduce its legal exposure for challenge.

TEC recommends adding the following language to (f)(9):

                   This subsection is optional for electric cooperatives and municipally

                   owned utilities. Electric cooperatives and municipally owned

                   utilities shall pass along the costs of direct interconnection to the

                   large load consumer in an appropriate manner solely determined by

                   the electric cooperative or MOU.

           TEC also notes that there is inconsistency in the treatment of CIAC in subsection (f)(9)(C)

as compared to subsection (g)(5).20 If the CIAC is subject to true up, it resembles a cash deposit.

If the intention is that CIAC is nonrefundable except in the situation where facilities are completed

and energized, that should be clearly stated. Additionally, if CIAC is not refundable in the event


19
     PFP at 24 (Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(f)(9)).
20
     PFP at 27 (Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(g)(5)).


                                                                                                   14
 the project is withdrawn or reduced, the affected TDSP(s) might have additional funds beyond the

amounts spent designing and/or constructing interconnecting facilities. TEC’s concerns identified

above regarding the problems with fees assessed to large loads to offset a TSP’s rate base would

apply to any excess CIAC funds as well.

           Finally, additional clarity is needed regarding the final treatment of the cost of significant

equipment or services as discussed in subsections (d)(11) and (f)(8) once facilities are completed

and energized.21 Presumably, the cost of the equipment should be assessed to the large load

customer in keeping with the spirit of Senate Bill 6, but that is not clearly stated in the proposed

rule.

9.         Other Novel Proposals Require Vetting

           TEC is aware that parties may propose new approaches to the framework for financial

commitments or the recovery of system costs in their comments in this proceeding. These

proposals, if they are novel to the rule, necessitate full review with an opportunity for stakeholder

comment. TEC therefore requests that the Commission allow further public comment on the rule

if the next iteration includes substantial deviations from the Proposal for Publication.

                                              II.      Conclusion

           TEC appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the proposed rule and looks

forward to working with the Commission and other stakeholders on this project.




21
     PFP at 15 and 23 (Proposed 16 TAC §§ 25.194(d)(11) & 25.194(f)(8)).

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                          §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                       §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                   §                     OF TEXAS


                             EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF
                        TEXAS ELECTRIC COOPERATIVES, INC.

Texas Electric Cooperatives, Inc. makes the following recommendations:

1)     The applicability in proposed §25.194 (b)(3) should be revised as follows:

              (3) an expanded interconnection that results in the total load at a
              single site reaching a new multiple of 75 MW.

2)     Additional guardrails are needed for loads that exceed their contract peak demand.

3)     The rule should clarify the division of study responsibilities between ERCOT, the TSP,
       and the DSP.

4)     Clarity is needed on the definition of system costs, and methods to allocate transmission
       costs should be aligned between projects.

5)     DSPs must have the ability to participate in any agreement with a customer located in their
       service area and maintain ownership over any necessary distribution facilities.

6)     TEC recommends that the Commission consider reducing the intermediate agreement
       security payment while increasing the required interconnection fee.

7)     The Commission should give parties 60 calendar days following the completion of the
       interconnection studies to enter into an interconnection agreement.

8)     The rule should clarify that the form of a posted letter of credit must meet the needs of the
       TSP/DSP.

9)     To ensure that other consumers are not bearing the costs of large load interconnections,
       while allowing the utility to earn an appropriate return, TEC recommends that the
       Commission consider removing the offset issue into a separate rulemaking to fully vet all
       available options.

10)    To comply with the statutory mandate that cooperatives may pass through costs in a manner
       determined by the cooperative, TEC recommends adding the following language to (f)(9):

              This subsection is optional for electric cooperatives and municipally
              owned utilities. Electric cooperatives and municipally owned


                                                                                                 17
           utilities shall pass along the costs of direct interconnection to the
          large load consumer in an appropriate manner solely determined by
          the electric cooperative or MOU.

11)   Should the rule change substantially, TEC asks for another opportunity
      to provide written comment.

                                                                                                1
                                        COMMENTS OF
                             TEXAS ELECTRIC COOPERATIVES, INC.

         Texas Electric Cooperatives, Inc. (TEC) respectfully submits these comments in response

to the proposal for publication (PFP) regarding large load interconnection standards (LLIS).1 TEC

is the statewide association of electric cooperatives operating in Texas, representing its members

except as their interests may be separately represented.2 The PFP directed comments to be filed by

April 17. These comments are timely filed.


                                                I.       Comments

1.       Applicability Clarification

         TEC recommends that proposed subsection § 25.194 (b)(3) be clarified.3 TEC understands

the Commission' s intent that expansions of an existing interconnection should trigger these large

6.      Financial Security and Refund Scenarios

        It is essential that ERCOT only plans for legitimate large loads that have a high likelihood

of sustained operations. It is also essential that new large load consumers bear the direct costs

associated with their interconnections to and use of the transmission system and that cost shifting

to other consumer classes be avoided. TEC is therefore generally supportive of the financial

security requirements placed on potential large load consumers throughout the proposed rule.

However, TEC is concerned that the posting of a large financial security requirement prior to the

completion of an interconnection study is overly punitive, because at this point the load lacks full

information on the potential costs associated with the interconnection and the transmission

capacity that ERCOT will allocate to the load.

        The potential for forfeiting large payments is substantial. Large loads that do not enter into

an interconnection agreement within 30 days of the completion of the study or that miss certain

milestones after entering an interconnection agreement would forfeit 80% of all security

payments: TEC notes that there may be legitimate factors beyond the load' s control that cause it

to miss a milestone or the 30-day interconnection deadline. From the electric provider perspective,

the 30-day deadline may also pose challenges for smaller entities and inhibit thorough due

diligence. TEC therefore recommends lowering and making refundable the financial security

requirement for the pre-study intermediate agreement to allow large load consumers and utilities

        TEC believes that the ability to demonstrate financial surety is key to being able to

7.      Offsetting TSP Rate Base

        Throughout the proposed rule TSPs are instructed to use funds from the large load

consumer to offset their costs in rate base.11 While TEC understands and supports the general

intention behind these provisions to prevent large load costs from being passed along to other

consumers, TEC is opposed to these provisions as mandated rate base offsets, because removing

these costs entirely from rate base will also prevent the utility from earning a return on facilities

and equipment on which it is statutorily authorized to earn such a return. A TSP' s ability to earn a

rate of return on its rate base is critical to its ability to function as a TSP.

        The current draft does not require large loads to pay for the on-going costs of operating

and maintaining transmission built to serve large loads or the costs of upgrades. TEC supports this

position. Administration of charges for 0&M costs assessed to large loads would be burdensome.




11 PFP at 23, 27, and 29 (Proposed 16 TAC §§ 25.194(f)(7)(B), 25.194(g)(4), & 25.194(h)(4)).


                                                                                                     10
 Furthermore, once the transmission equipment is built, it willlikely benefit the entire grid. Utilities

should therefore be able to recover the associated costs of the upgrades to and operation and

maintenance of these facilities as part of their rates.

        Additionally, for some transmission providers, these large rate base offsets may

significantly eat into the overall rate base of the utility, reducing or in some cases potentially

eliminating its rate base entirely, significantly skewing the utility' s financial standing. Even a

larger TSP may be detrimentally impacted by this requirement given the number of large loads

which have indicated interest in interconnection. For example, if a TSP signs interconnection

agreements forjust ten large loads of 1,000 MW each, that would be $500,000,000 in fees collected

(10 X 1,000 MW X $50,000/MW). This could easily be half of a TSP's rate base.

        While the TSP would still be collecting the fees from the large loads, collection of the fees

is far different than earning a rate of return on rate base. A TSP would only be able to earn interest

on the money deposited, a percentage significantly lower than the typical TSP rate of return. A

TSP' s debt service requirements are based upon expected rate recovery. A significant reduction in

rate base may, therefore, lead to a violation of a TSP's loan covenants, putting its financing, and

thus, its financial future, in jeopardy. Additionally, the TSP would have insufficient funds to

design, construct, maintain and operate its system. The TSP would not have the ability to raise its

rates to support its necessary activities without a rate proceeding in front of the Commission. If a

TSP must raise its rates to continue to operate, then the benefit of any offset would be defeated.

        Even if the fees collected were lowered and the risk of financial impact to TSPs averted,

the additional administration of any sort of offset would be a significant additional accounting

burden for every TSP in the ERCOT region which received the fees. The offset would require

special accounting treatment and would need to be recovered over the course of many years.




                                                                                                     11
           There are numerous options available to offset the costs to other consumers for the

interconnection of a large load that do not impact the TSP rate base. These options range from an

offsetting of the ERCOT administration fee that can then be ultimately credited back to consumers,

or an offset to the annual TCOS charges. TEC is not advocating for any specific credit or offset

policy but recommends that the Commission consider taking this specific issue into consideration

through a separate rulemaking to fully vet all of the available options and ensure that consumers

are protected while TSPs have the funding necessary to operate and maintain the transmission

system.

          Clarity is also needed for when a large load leaves the interconnection process, and ERCOT

is charged with re-allocating what has become underutilized capacity. The new load to which the

underutilized capacity is allocated must also post surety to avoid leaving a gap in posted security

for the upgrades. The current draft of the rule does not specifically cover this gap and makes it

much more likely that the additional amounts will be recovered through existing mechanisms-

other customers-rather than the large load that steps into the shoes of the large load that has exited

the process.

recovery method for the direct costs of the interconnection on electric cooperatives and

municipally owned utilities (MOU).12 Electric cooperatives and MOUs continue to retain sole

jurisdiction over their rates and methods of recovery.13 Senate Bill 6 added an additional provision

to protect cooperatives and MOUs in PURA § 35.004(c-2), which specifically reinforces electric
